title: Electricity
seo_title: Year 8 Science: Electricity Worksheets (Current, Voltage, Resistance, Static)
standard_text: Electric current, measured in amperes, in circuits, series and parallel circuits, currents add where branches meet and current as flow of charge; potential difference, measured in volts, battery and bulb ratings; resistance, measured in ohms, as the ratio of potential difference (p.d.) to current; differences in resistance between conducting and insulating components (quantitative); static electricity: separation of positive or negative charges when objects are rubbed together, transfer of electrons, forces between charged objects; the idea of electric field, forces acting across the space between objects not in contact.
meta_desc: Free Year 8 science worksheets on electricity: current and potential difference, ammeters and voltmeters, series and parallel circuits, resistance R = V ÷ I and static electricity. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: In series current is the same everywhere; in parallel branch currents add up.
body_html:
How to think about it

Current is the flow of charge; potential difference is the push.

  • Series: the current is the same everywhere; the potential difference is shared.
  • Parallel: the branch currents add up to the total; each branch gets the full potential difference.
  • Resistance R = V ÷ I, in ohms. Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.
Example

6 V across a lamp, 0.5 A through it. R?

R = 6 ÷ 0.5

Answer: 12 Ω

Example

Branches carry 0.3 A and 0.2 A. Total?

Add in parallel

Answer: 0.5 A

Common mistakes

  • Thinking current is used up by a lamp.
  • Connecting a voltmeter in series.
  • Thinking like charges attract.

faq.q: What is the difference between current and potential difference?
faq.a: Current is the flow of charge, measured in amps with an ammeter in series. Potential difference is the push, measured in volts with a voltmeter in parallel.
Divide the potential difference by the current: R = V ÷ I. The unit is the ohm (Ω).
Rubbing two materials moves electrons from one to the other. The one gaining electrons becomes negative; like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
